title: How to Reduce Pet Dander in Your HVAC System
h1: How Can I Reduce Pet Dander in My HVAC System?
description: Pet dander rides through your ducts to every room. Learn which filters, cleaning habits and air quality upgrades actually cut dander from your HVAC system.
quick_answer: Use a pleated filter rated to catch fine particles, change it more often than the label says, and keep return grilles free of hair. Groom pets regularly and vacuum with a HEPA vacuum. If allergies persist, have the ducts cleaned and consider a whole-home air cleaner sized for your system.
body:
How does pet dander get into the HVAC system?

Dander is tiny flakes of skin, plus dried saliva and urine proteins, that pets shed constantly. It's light enough to hang in the air and sticky enough to cling to fabric, walls and the inside of ductwork. Every time the system runs, the return grilles pull room air, and the dander in it, toward the filter.

Whatever the filter misses gets blown back out to every room. Over time, dander and hair also coat the blower wheel and the inside of the return duct, which can keep stirring allergens back into the air even after a good cleaning of the house.

What filter is best for pet dander?

A pleated filter does far more than the thin fiberglass type. For homes with pets, look for a filter labeled for fine particles or pet allergens, in the exact size your system takes.

  • Change it more often. With one pet, every 30 to 60 days is a reasonable target. With several pets or a heavy shedder, check it monthly.
  • Don't oversize the rating. Very dense filters can restrict airflow on some systems and make the blower work harder. If you want higher filtration, a thicker media filter cabinet is usually the better route.
  • Make sure it seals. Hair and dander will happily go around a loose filter.

Pull the filter out and hold it up to a light when you check it. If you can barely see light through it, or it's matted with hair on the intake side, it's done. Keep a few spares in the right size on hand so a change never waits on a trip to the store.

What daily habits cut down on dander?

The less dander that gets into the air, the less your system has to catch. These help the most:

  1. Brush pets often, ideally outside or in the garage, and bathe them as your vet recommends.
  2. Vacuum the return grilles every couple of weeks. Hair builds up on them fast and blocks airflow.
  3. Use a HEPA vacuum on carpets, rugs and furniture at least weekly.
  4. Wash pet bedding and throw blankets in hot water regularly.
  5. Keep pets out of the bedroom of anyone with allergies, and keep that door closed.
  6. Move pet beds away from the return grille. A dog bed right in front of the return feeds hair straight into the system.

Does duct cleaning help with pet allergies?

It can, especially if you've had pets for years, just moved into a home where the last owners had pets, or you can see hair and debris when you pull off a vent cover. Cleaning removes the built-up layer that keeps shedding allergens back into the airflow.

It works best when paired with a better filter and a clean blower. If the blower wheel and coil are coated, cleaning the ducts alone won't solve it.

Are air purifiers worth it for pet owners?

For people with real allergy symptoms, they're often worth a look. There are two main options:

  • Whole-home media air cleaners mount at the furnace or air handler and filter all the air the system moves. They hold far more dander than a standard 1-inch filter and don't need changing as often.
  • Portable HEPA purifiers are good for a single bedroom. Size them for the room and run them continuously.

Keep in mind a whole-home cleaner only works while the fan is running. Some homeowners run the fan more often during heavy shedding seasons for that reason. Our indoor air quality team can look at your system and suggest what fits.

Does Southern California weather make dander worse?

Dry inland air, especially during Santa Ana winds, can make skin and sinuses more irritated, so the same amount of dander feels worse. Many pets also shed heavily as the weather warms in spring. Keeping indoor humidity in a comfortable middle range and staying ahead on filter changes during those stretches helps a lot. If your ducts haven't been looked at in a while, our duct cleaning service is a good place to start.
faqs: How often should I change my air filter if I have pets?

With one pet, plan on every 30 to 60 days for a standard 1-inch pleated filter. With multiple pets, heavy shedders or someone with allergies in the house, check it monthly and change it when it looks gray or furry.
Can pet hair damage my HVAC system?
It can over time. Hair clogs filters, coats the blower wheel and sticks to the indoor coil, all of which reduce airflow. Less airflow means longer run times, higher bills and more wear on the system.
Do UV lights kill pet dander?
No. UV lights are aimed at mold and bacteria growing on the coil. Dander is a particle, so it needs to be filtered out of the air rather than treated with light.
Is it worth cleaning ducts after getting a new pet?

Not right away. Duct cleaning makes more sense after years of pets, when you move into a home that had pets, or if you see hair and debris inside the ducts. Start with better filters and grille cleaning.
